blocks.text: But others render it βασιλίσκον [basiliskon], or regulus, as Jerome does, and those same Greeks at Es. LIX, 5. Others render it ἔχιδναν [echidnan], viper, as Aquila does, and the same Jerome in [III, 127] Job and at Es. XXX, 6. The Chaldee sometimes has תנינא, dragon, sometimes חיון, serpent, sometimes חרמנין מפרחין, flying snakes. And the Syriac in one place has ܚܘܝܘܢܐ, little snake, and the Arabic الحية الجردا [al-ḥayya al-jardā] smooth serpent, which is also called by another name, الاقرع [al-aqraʿ] bald. Hence Alcamus: الاقرع من الحيات متعط شعر راسه لكثرة سمه [al-aqraʿ min al-ḥayyāt mutamaʿʿiṭ shaʿr raʾsihi li-kathrat summihi] The bald one among serpents is the one that is stripped of the hair of its head because of the abundance of its poison. Thus hardly anything certain about this word can be drawn from the ancient versions of Scripture.

Among the masters of the Hebrews there is the same hesitation here. אפעה ephe is rendered by Solomon on Job as burning serpent, that is, prester; by Mordecai and Pomarius as the serpent which infects by its look alone, that is, the regulus or basilisk. That [col. 360] Kimchi was of this opinion one might gather from the fact that on Es. XXX he makes אפעה ephe and צפעוני tsiphoni synonyms. Yet he seems rather to mean the cenchrites, since elsewhere the same author describes אפעה ephe as a serpent with a variegated and spotted skin, following the opinion of R. Meir, which rests on the authority of the Chaldee paraphrase, where אפעיא stand for הצבועים, that is, as some would have it, painted and spotted serpents, 1 Sam. XIII, 18. I pass over the trifles of the Talmudists: that in the carob tree, every seventieth year, two serpents of this species are generated, one of each sex, the male being called צבוע and the female נפרוא, and that nature stops here as if by deliberate design, so that this plague may not grow worse through excessive loss of life.

In this crowd of interpreters I do not doubt that the laurel must go to Aquila, for whom אפעה ephe is the viper. Many of the more recent scholars rightly follow him, since it is a well-established fact that even today among the Arabs الافعي [al-afʿī] alephe means viper. This is clear not only from the Arabic paraphrase of the New Testament, in which الافعي [al-afʿī] alephe, that is, the viper, fastens itself on Paul's hand, Act. XXVIII, 3, and the Pharisees are repeatedly ^{a)} called اولاد الافاعي [awlād al-afāʿī] offspring of alaphai, that is, of vipers, but also from the books of the physicians. Thus Avicenna, in book 2 of the Canon, prescribes ابوجلسا [abūjalsā] or شنجار [shinjār] anchusa, and اناجلس [anājalis] anagallis, and لوف [lūf] dracontium, and كرسنة [kirsanna] bitter vetch, and قسط [qusṭ] costus, and حسك [ḥasak] caltrop, and كرم [karm] the vine, and فاشرا [fāshirā] bryony, and بول الانسان [bawl al-insān] human urine against the bite of الافاعي [al-afāʿī] alaphai, that is, of vipers. For all these are taken from Dioscorides, who recommends the same remedies for ἐχιοδήκτοις [echiodēktois]. The same Avicenna reports ^{b)} that the fat of [III, 128] الافعي [al-afʿī] alephe is an effective remedy against dimness of the eyes, and he orders its flesh to be used for the treatment of leprosy ^{c)}. These very powers are attributed to the flesh and fat of the viper by Dioscorides, Galen, Paul and Aëtius. Finally, that the word افعي [afʿī] ephe is used for the viper will be clearer than daylight to anyone who compares the writings of the Greeks with Avicenna's treatises On leprosy, On theriac, and On the bite of الافاعي [al-afāʿī] alaphai ^{(1)}.
